Beyond Lavender and Olives: Greece’s Emerging Garden Style

Home
Inspired Gardens and Design
Articles: Beyond Lavender and Olives: Greece’s Emerging Garden Style

Contributor

Saxon Holt
  • Topics: Inspired Gardens and Design, Sustainable Gardening

Autumn 2026 

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:02
Instaread

Greece has an iconic summer-dry climate. When we traveled from the mediterranean West Coast to capital-M Mediterranean Greece on the recent Pacific Horticulture tour, we assumed we would be seeing the choicest Mediterranean plants in their native settings, and gardens that represented a long horticultural tradition of working with these plants. We did not realize that Greece does not have a long history of ornamental horticulture.

Unlike other Mediterranean countries such as Spain,  France, and Italy that have a long history of treating landscape architecture as an art, subsidized by aristocracy and royal families, Greece has remained distinctly agricultural and decidedly poorer. That extends to today, where there is not a large middle class with the leisure time to have ornamental gardens.

That is changing in real time with the influence of British people who have second homes in Greece, and local horticulturists who are exploring native plants. Together, they are creating distinctive gardens that can benefit any of us who garden in summer-dry climates.

Appropriately, we started our tour in Corfu, the setting of the real-life story of The Durrells in Corfu, a popular British Masterpiece series a few years back.

We soon learned Corfu, despite its distinctly Mediterranean climate, receives more annual rainfall than London, and British expatriates have developed an ornamental garden style with an increasing use of Greek native plants.

All images courtesy of Saxon Holt

Greek communities are largely agrarian, practicing traditional gardening skills for cultivating olives and vegetables for their rich culinary heritage. That is changing with English influences that focus more on formality and design, with garden rooms, meandering pathways, and stone walls to define garden spaces.

We toured several gardens on Corfu designed by Greek-based but British-born Jennifer Gay. She takes these classic design ideas then adapts them to the Mediterranean plant palette, creating a real sense of place.

Most of the gardeners on the tour recognized the classic Mediterranean, summer-dry plant palette using lavenders (Lavandula spp.), rockroses (Cistus spp.) and olives (Olea europaea) that we would expect to look quite at home in Greek gardens. We were surprised to also find non-traditional native plants and wildflowers in local gardens.

The native flora of Greece became the highlight of our trip and we spent several days touring native habitats with our guide, Elefteris Dariotis, the renowned Greek horticulturist.

Once we left Corfu, we traveled across the country, touring special sites such as Vikos Gorge in the Zagori region. We stayed a few days in the Pelion Peninsula and then flew to Crete from Thessaloníki.

Crete was a revelation.

We understood from a historical standpoint that Greece was an ancient civilization. This was where Western civilization’s study of science began, pioneered by people such as Aristotle’s contemporary Theophrastus, the father of botany. But here we were, staying in a lovely modern hotel in the bustling but ancient city of Chania that Minoans settled 2,000 years before Theophrastus.

An island in the Mediterranean, smack in the middle of some of the earliest sailing routes. Of course Crete has a long history.

Crete is also quite beautiful, rugged, and full of a distinctive native flora. Elefteris brought us here to show us the White Mountains. This international hotspot for biodiversity is recognized as a Global Centre of Plant Diversity, with 650 different species of plants, of which 97 are endemic to Crete (Cretan Flora 2020).

Centuries of olive farming and goat grazing have changed many of the native habitats, but during our tour along winding mountain roads we found roadside wonders, including this Cretan ebony (Ebonus creticus).

Elefteris has a nursery in Crete, exploring the island whenever he can, so he knows special locations where fencing has kept the goats out. One such small field on Omalos Plateau hosts Tulipa × bakeri, a naturally occurring hybrid of Candia tulip (T. saxitilis) and Cretan rock tulip (T. cretica), a tulip that is only known on Crete. He also knew of a lovely trail where we could take a long hike to find the rare Crete peony (Paeonia clusii), but apparently, we were about 10 days too early this year. As it turned out, we were able to see it—planted in the front parking lot of the taverna where we had lunch.

After we left Crete for Athens for the final leg of our tour, Elefteris’s passion for the region’s native plants was on full display. We had plans to see two of the most influential gardens around Athens: Sparoza, the home of the Mediterranean Garden Society, and the Vorres Museum, which has transformed its gardens with climate-adapted Mediterranean plants.

However, because the Vorres Museum is in the town of Paiania, outside of Athens, we were able to squeeze in a short visit to Elefteris’ own garden and nursery, the backyard and side lot of his parents’ home, also in Paiania. His enthusiasm for these very special plants is infectious.

It is astounding how small the garden really is given the number of plants he has been able to grow that he shares with customers and landscape designers throughout Greece. We were also amazed by the small shed-office that he uses to clean and organize the seeds, which he collects on his various botanizing trips and then sells to customers around the world.

When we arrived at the Vorres Museum, we learned that not only have they started using more Mediterranean plants throughout their formal gardens, they also have a large test area where Elefteris trials plants and lets them grow with no summer irrigation.

The Dry Garden test area behind the museum is not a public space and there’s no formal garden design, just garden beds with a lot of different plants, mostly Greek natives. Many of these plants are already in horticulture, but few people realize they are from Greece. These trials show how well they work together and suggest new pairings with a distinctively Greek aesthetic.

This is a very conscious part of his work to elevate Greek gardens in general. Elefteris is already influencing other gardens around the country, as we will see in our next stop.

Perhaps the highlight of the entire trip was the tour of Sparoza garden, the headquarters of the Mediterranean Garden Society. Our special guide Lucie Willan, who until quite recently was head gardener, helped update the garden with a diverse collection of Mediterranean and Greek native plants that are beautifully maintained.

Willan is an English transplant who worked in classic English gardens such as Sissinghurst and Hidcote before discovering Greece and its incredible biodiversity and making it her new home. She brought her keen plantsmanship and a sense of formality to Sparoza using climate-adapted plants, helping to create a horticultural style that Greece has lacked.

Note the careful pruning of the three plants below: the mastic tree (Pistacia lentiscus) and its deep bronzy green against the stone wall, combined with the rounded, gray foliage of shrubby germander (Teucrium fruticans ‘Agadir’) just beyond, down the path. Renowned French nurseryman Olivier Filippi first selected the cultivar ‘Agadir’ for its compact growth habit, a well-chosen plant for its adaptability to this sort of shaping.

In the foreground is Cretan pincushion flower (Lomelosia cretica, syn. Scabiosa cretica), another carefully selected plant used in gardens for its compact size and adaptability to shearing. The three plants placed together along this wandering path create a fascinating rhythm of distinctive plants, inviting admiration as one strolls the garden.

The careful choice of cultivars in Sparoza Garden is also seen in this grouping of Boule rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus ‘Boule’) and Greek spiny spurge (Euphorbia acanthothamnus) along a path behind a main house.

The chartreuse green of this totally wild-looking euphorbia mounds beautifully next to the rosemary. The Boule rosemary is a semi-upright variety that forms a compact mound and maintains a clean and formal pruned appearance with very minimal effort.

Sparoza is a showcase of what gardeners can do in very tough and hot summer-dry locations, and I think each gardener on our tour came away inspired.

These are exciting times in Greek horticulture. Clearly a horticultural style is developing beyond using Mediterranean plants in ornamental settings within classic garden design motifs. There’s a conscious movement to use native plants.

This is exciting for gardeners in the Pacific Horticulture region, too. No doubt, as these plants are cultivated and tried in gardens, the best will find their way here. Our own palette of Mediterranean plants will expand. Perhaps we were looking at a bit of our own future.

We rounded out our garden tours with Greek history in Athens, visiting Poseidon’s Temple and the Parthenon on the ancient Acropolis. These sprawling temple grounds float above the modern skyline—as we saw from our farewell dinner on our last night together.

Let’s end the story with a group photo. When we were on Corfu, we took a brief stop overlooking the sea and the real-life home of the Durrell family of Masterpiece fame: Durrells in Corfu.

Resources

Lenton, Steve. 2020. Cretan Flora
